title: Mizzou’s Eli Drinkwitz blasts Kansas’ ‘Border War’ video depicting rivalry’s Civil War origins
content:
LAWRENCE, Kan. — A hype video released by Kansas earlier this week that illuminated the sordid origins of the Missouri-Kansas “Border War” left Missouri coach Eli Drinkwitz questioning whether the football rivalry should be played again.

After his Tigers’ 38-21 win over the Jayhawks on Friday night at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium, Drinkwitz said, “I don’t really care if it continues or not.”

“If they’re going to be weird about it, then what’s the point?” Drinkwitz said. “… If they want to have a football game and play the football game, a great rivalry on the border, then awesome, let’s do it. But if they want to make it deeper than that, we left Kansas bleeding again and call it good.”

On Thursday afternoon, Kansas released a one-minute, 29-second video that included phrases such as “heroes and villains” and “right and wrong” and depicted images and figures from the region’s tumultuous past.

During the Civil War, Kansas was a free state on the Union side, while Missouri also remained in the Union but was split between the factions. On Aug. 21, 1863, Confederate guerrillas from Missouri led by William Quantrill sacked Lawrence and killed around 150 men. Kansas’ Jayhawkers committed violence of their own on the Missouri side — hence the rivalry’s name.

The video had received more than 32 million views by the end of Friday’s game.

“I was disappointed in the rivalry, the turn that it took today,” Drinkwitz said. “I thought that was uncalled for, and this is about two teams playing football. … Everybody’s got complicated pasts, and to make that an icon was bizarre to me.”

Missouri-Kansas was the second-most played FBS rivalry when the Tigers left the Big 12 for the SEC in 2012. Kansas vowed not to play Missouri again and didn’t relent on the football field until last year, when the sides met in Columbia. This was the second of a two-game contract between the foes, and they’re scheduled to meet again in 2031 and 2032.

Drinkwitz also took issue with the video’s timing. Kansas and Missouri played on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, the Washington, D.C., area and Pennsylvania. There was a moment of silence in remembrance and a military flyover before kickoff.

“I’m just glad that this whole right-versus-wrong bull crap that was started just got settled,” Drinkwitz said. “… It’s a football game. It’s an American football game. People love to come watch and cheer for their teams. It’s not even deeper than that. And I get there’s a past for it, but why are we stirring that bull crap up? It’s 9/11. This country needs unity now more than ever. And I was embarrassed for them, to be honest. That’s why I tried to embarrass them at the end.”

With 34 seconds left in the game, Missouri took over at Kansas’ 13-yard line. Instead of kneeling the ball, the Tigers on their first play threw a pass into the end zone, which fell incomplete. The second play was a run that gained 6 yards and ended the contest.

“I didn’t want to score too bad or I’d have called timeouts and tried,” Drinkwitz said. “We didn’t think we were going to throw that in the end zone, but I just wanted to let them know.”
